title: The Spinal Cord & Reflex Arcs: Neural Highways & Involuntary Action
description: Master the cross-sectional anatomy of the spinal cord (dorsal vs. ventral horns), afferent vs. efferent tracts, and monosynaptic/polysynaptic reflexes.

slides.title: Spinal Cord Anatomy: The Butterfly Core 🦋
slides.content:
# The Central Information Superhighway

The spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum of the skull down to the lumbar region (terminating at the conus medullaris around L1-L2). A cross-section reveals:

* **Inner Gray Matter**: H-shaped or butterfly-shaped region packed with neuronal cell bodies and unmyelinated interneurons.
  * **Dorsal Horns**: Contain sensory nuclei receiving inputs from sensory neurons.
  * **Ventral Horns**: Contain large motor neuron cell bodies whose axons command skeletal muscles.
* **Outer White Matter**: Myelinated fiber tracts carrying information up and down the neuraxis.
  * **Ascending Tracts**: Sensory highways traveling upward to the brain (e.g., Dorsal Columns, Spinothalamic tract).
  * **Descending Tracts**: Motor highways carrying commands downward from the brain (e.g., Corticospinal tract).

quizData.question: According to the Bell-Magendie Law of spinal nerve roots, what type of signals travel through the dorsal and ventral roots?

options.text: Dorsal roots are motor (efferent); ventral roots are sensory (afferent)
Dorsal roots are sensory (afferent); ventral roots are motor (efferent)
Both dorsal and ventral roots carry identical mixed signals
Dorsal roots control autonomic digestion; ventral roots control conscious thought

quizData.explanation: The Bell-Magendie Law dictates: Dorsal = Sensory (Afferent) inputs entering the cord; Ventral = Motor (Efferent) outputs exiting to muscles.

slides.title: Reflex Arcs: Survival Without Brain Delays ⚡
slides.content:
## Reflex Circuitry

A **reflex** is an involuntary, stereotyped motor response to a sensory stimulus that can occur without conscious brain intervention.

### The Patellar (Knee-Jerk) Reflex — Monosynaptic:
1. Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps muscle.
2. **Muscle spindles** detect the stretch and fire action potentials along **Ia sensory afferents**.
3. Sensory afferent enters the dorsal horn and synapses *directly* onto an **alpha motor neuron** in the ventral horn (no interneuron = monosynaptic!).
4. Motor neuron fires, contracting the quadriceps and causing the lower leg to kick forward.

### The Withdrawal (Flexor) Reflex — Polysynaptic:
Stepping on a painful nail excites pain nociceptors, which synapse on excitatory and inhibitory spinal interneurons. Interneurons simultaneously contract the ipsilateral flexor muscles (withdrawing the foot) and extend the contralateral leg (crossed-extensor reflex) so you don't collapse!

quizData.question: Why is the patellar tendon stretch reflex classified as a 'monosynaptic' reflex?

options.text: It requires only one single neurotransmitter molecule to complete
The sensory afferent neuron synapses directly onto the motor neuron without an intermediate interneuron
It only fires once in a person's lifetime
It is completely mediated within a single brain hemisphere

quizData.explanation: A monosynaptic reflex contains only one single central synapse between the primary sensory afferent and the alpha motor neuron.
